title: Antioxidant taurine inhibits chondrocyte ferroptosis through upregulation of OGT/Gpx4 signaling in osteoarthritis induced by anterior cruciate ligament transection

sections.abstract: Keywords: Taurine, Osteoarthritis, Oxidative stress, O-GlcNAcylation, Ferroptosis
sections.introduction:
Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic inflammatory joint disease characterized by cartilage degradation, synovial inflammation, and subchondral bone remodeling. Patients with OA often experience discomfort such as joint pain, swelling, stiffness, and impaired mobility, which can lead to joint deformity and disability in severe cases, imposing heavy burdens on the patient's family and society [1] . Although the benefits of physical activity are well known, previous studies have shown that 30 % of the world's population does not reach the level of physical activity recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) [2] . In 2012, Hallal et al. reported that about 31 % of adults and about 80 % of adolescents were categorized as physically inactive globally [3] . In recent years, as the concept of “the nationwide body-building” has gained popularity, people's enthusiasm for participating in sports has increased, especially among the adolescent population, which has also led to a rapid increase in the number of sports injury cases [4] . An estimated 250,000 anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur each year in the United States, resulting in decreased sports participation and joint dysfunction [5] . Traumatic joint injury is an important risk factor for post-traumatic OA (PTOA). Previous studies have found that the incidence of knee PTOA after ACL injury is 4.2 times higher than in uninjured individuals [6] . It has been estimated that halving the incidence of knee OA following ACL injuries would result in an annual cost savings of $1.1 billion in the United States alone [5] . As a common sports injury, PTOA secondary to ACL injury has received extensive attention [7] . However, there is no effective clinical strategy to completely reverse the course of PTOA. At present, the clinical management of OA consists mainly of pharmacologic and surgical treatments. Due to the absence of approved disease-modifying drugs (DMOADs), pharmacological treatment is mainly based on pain-relieving nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which usually have gastrointestinal side effects as well as cardiovascular or renal risks, even electrolyte disturbances and renal failure in severe cases [8] . Surgical treatment is only chosen when patients have unrelieved pain in advanced stages of OA, due to the trauma associated with surgery and its potential complications [9] . In addition, some clinical practices have suggested that platelet-rich plasma (PRP) strategies have shown good potential to promote cartilage regeneration in PTOA. However, the preparation and use of PRP also carries some risk of infection. Moreover, there is also a lack of sufficient clinical evidence that PRP is effective in delaying OA progression [10] . In general, currently, effective strategies to reverse the pathologic changes in PTOA are lacking. Cumulative evidence suggests that PTOA is a unique OA phenotype, suggesting that more targeted therapeutic strategies may exist for PTOA. This hypothesis was confirmed at the molecular pathophysiologic level [11] , [12] . Unlike other types of OA, PTOA secondary to sports injury has well-defined injury events such as ACL injury, meniscus tear, and patellar dislocation. This clear “starting point” event opens up the possibility of targeted treatment of PTOA, enables timely detection and assessment of the extent of joint damage and pathologic progression after a joint injury to guide and modify treatment strategies, thereby preventing knee cartilage degeneration and irreversible joint damage [7] . However, how to prevent secondary OA scientifically and effectively after ACL injury is a stifling problem.

Metabolomics, as an emerging research tool in life science research, can instantly reflect and understand the dynamic changes in cell physiology and pathology through high-throughput detection and analysis of small molecule substrates, intermediates and end products of cellular metabolism, thus explaining the intrinsic mechanisms in the process of disease initiation and progression from a metabolic perspective [13] . Therefore, by exploring the changing patterns of key metabolic molecules and related metabolic pathways in the progression of OA disease, it is promising to screen meaningful PTOA-related metabolic markers or identify promising therapeutic targets. However, single-omics studies that can only correlate the disease mainly reflect changes in the disease process without explaining causality [14] . In our study, we combined metabolomics and transcriptomics to perform a multi-omics analysis of inflammatory chondrocytes to explore the underlying mechanisms of OA progression. The benefit of multi-omics is that one omics technique can compensate for the shortcomings of another to provide a comprehensive overview of molecular complexity, leading to a more complete understanding of the molecular changes that lead to disease [15] . However, highthroughput screening technologies can only provide predictions about molecular regulatory networks based on highly complex computational analyses. Therefore, more in-depth molecular biology approaches are necessary to fully validate the results of the omics technologies.

Recent reports suggest a possible link between ferroptosis and pathologic changes in OA [16] . Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of non-apoptotic cell death [16] . Unlike other forms of cell death such as necrosis, apoptosis, or autophagy, ferroptosis has unique morphological, biochemical, genetic, and immunological characteristics [17] . Ferroptosis has been reported to be caused by a redox imbalance produced by oxidants and antioxidants, which is characterized by the accumulation of large amounts of iron-dependent lipid excesses of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (mainly including hydrogen peroxide, superoxide, and hydroxyl radicals), leading to cellular damage, decreased cell viability, and even cell death [17] , [18] . Accumulation of ROS is necessary for ferroptosis [16] , [19] . Previous studies have shown that glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4) is a key regulator of ferroptosis [20] . Wang et al. [21] showed that inhibition of Piezo1 protein activity increased Gpx4 expression and attenuated the ferroptosis phenotype, thereby alleviating OA progression in mice. Further, conditional knockdown of Gpx4 in cartilage exacerbated OA, whereas treatment with ferroptosis suppressor protein (FSP-1) and coenzyme Q10 attenuated OA progression in Gpx4 knockout mice. This suggests that Gpx4-mediated ferroptosis plays an important regulatory role in the initiation and progression of OA.

Taurine is a non-essential amino acid synthesized from methionine and cysteine by cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSD), which exists in a free state in the body and does not involved in protein synthesis [22] . As the most abundant free sulfur amino acid in the human body, taurine is widely distributed within human tissues, including the brain, pancreas, retina, neurons, bones, and muscles [23] . Although taurine can be biosynthesized in the liver and pancreas (taurine has also been found to be synthesized in nerve cells such as astrocytes and neurons, as well as in adipocytes), the human body relies heavily on taurine from dietary sources such as fish and meat [24] , [25] . Cumulative studies have shown that taurine is widely used as a potent antioxidant substance that plays an essential antioxidant role in a variety of diseases such as tumors, myocardial damage and osteoporosis [26] . A recent study published in Science journal reported that serum taurine levels gradually decrease with age. Taurine supplementation may be closely related to the prevention of many diseases, especially aging [27] . Thus, we speculated that taurine may play a chondroprotective role in PTOA lesions through antioxidant effects. Based on this, in this paper, we delved into the potential mechanisms by which taurine protects against cartilage degeneration through a multi-omics analysis. We hypothesized that taurine might alleviate chondrocyte inflammatory responses by modulating oxidative stress-related ferroptosis and O-GlcNAcylation. We preliminarily verified that the key protein for ferroptosis, Gpx4, may have O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT)-dependent O-GlcNAcylation, which is the first time to validate the existence of a direct relationship between Gpx4 and O-GlcNAcylation. Overall, we elucidated that taurine inhibits chondrocyte ferroptosis through upregulation of OGT/Gpx4 signaling, which will provide new directions for therapeutic strategies for PTOA. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first article to report the regulatory role of O-GlcNAcylation in OA both in vivo and in vitro , which will contribute a new idea of OA research, inspiring scholars to focus on other proteins that may harbor O-GlcNAcylation that may be involved in the regulation of OA initiation and progression.
sections.methods:
Seventy-two Sprague-Dawley (SD) healthy male rats weighing about 220 g were purchased from the Animal Experiment Center of Fujian Medical University. The rats were housed in the Laboratory Animal Center of Fujian Medical University (Ethics Approval No. [2018] No.005). The basic conditions of the rearing environment: the temperature was maintained at 23℃-25℃; the relative humidity was 40 %-60 %; artificial lighting was used, the time of natural light and darkness was alternated for 12 h; ordinary feed was fed; all the rats were allowed to eat and drink freely.

After 3 days of acclimatization, rats were randomly divided into 6 groups: 0 weeks postoperative group (0 W group, n = 12), 4 weeks postoperative group (4 W group, n = 12), 8 weeks postoperative group (8 W group, n = 12), 12 weeks postoperative group (12 W group, n = 12), 16 weeks postoperative group (16 W group, n = 12), and 20 weeks postoperative group (20 W group, n = 12). The knee joint of one hind limb of each group of rats received ACLT (ACLT group), while the contralateral knee joint served as a control (Sham group). The specific groupings of animal experiments are shown in Table 1 .

Animal experimental grouping.

The ACLT surgical procedure is based on previously published literature [44] and the accumulated experience of our laboratory. All rats were fasted for 12–24 h before surgery. Isoflurane was used to anesthetize rats. Rats could be operated after the toes were pinched without reaction. Rats were placed in supine position and fixed on the operating table. The surgical area was routinely sterilized. Rats were shaved around the knee joint. The skin was incised along the medial margin of the patellar ligament with a scalpel. The subcutaneous tissue and joint capsule were incised layer by layer. The fat pad tissue at the intercondylar fossa was bluntly separated to expose the intercondylar fossa until the ACL could be visualized. Subsequently, the ACL was cut using ophthalmic scissors. A drawer test is performed to confirm that the ACL has been completely severed. The operation should be performed gently to avoid damage to the articular cartilage and vascular nerves. The surgical incision was then closed with layer-by-layer sutures. The joint capsule of rats in the Sham group was incised and the joint cavity was exposed but the ACL was not clipped. Each rat was injected with penicillin intramuscularly (150,000 units each time, once a day for three days) after surgery to prevent infection. All rats were free to move around in the cage.

The rats in each group were fasted and watered for 12 h before being sacrificed. The rats were weighed. The rats were then anesthetized to death by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital according to their body weight. Soft tissues such as muscle ligaments around the knee joint were stripped, leaving the knee joint intact. 4 % paraformaldehyde was used to immobilize the knee joint for 36–48 h.

Eighty-four 10-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. All mice were housed in the Laboratory Animal Center of Xiamen University (Ethics Approval No. XMYY-2024KYSB081). After one week of acclimatization feeding, all mice were randomly divided into seven groups: Sham group (Sham group, n = 12); ACLT group (ACLT group, n = 12); ACLT + taurine administration group, (ACLT + Taur group, n = 12), ACLT + taurine + negative control for Gpx4 knockdown group (ACLT + Taur + NC-Gpx4 group, n = 12), ACLT + taurine + Gpx4 knockdown group (ACLT + Taur + AAV-sh-Gpx4 group, n = 12), ACLT + taurine + OSMI-1 administration group (ACLT + Taur + OSMI group, n = 12), and ACLT + taurine + TMG administration group (ACLT + Taur + TMG group, n = 12). The surgical procedure for ACLT in mice was basically the same as that for ACLT in rats. Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane during surgery. Taurine, AAV-sh-Gpx4, OSMI and TMG were administered by local injection into the knee joint cavity. Taurine (30 mg/kg, 5 μl per injection), OSMI (1 mg/kg, 5 μl per injection), and TMG (1 mg/kg, 5 μl per injection) were all administered twice weekly. All mice were sacrificed 8 weeks after ACLT surgery.

Micro-CT scanning of knee joints was performed with a Micro-CT scanner (SkyScan model 1076, Kontich, Belgium) [45] . The X-ray tube voltage in the instrument was 88 KV, the current through the tube was 100 μA, and the lead filter diameter was 1.0 mm. Scanning was performed at a rotation speed of 0.6° per rotation, with an exposure time of 560 ms per exposure and 180° scanning. All images were reconstructed using NRecon software and then retargeted using the Interactive Viewing and Analysis of Dynamic Data software. The intact bone tissue of the specimen was used as the region of interest (ROI) for 3D reconstruction. Bone structures within the ROI were selected for 3D visualization. Quantitative analysis Images and data were quantitatively analyzed with CTvol 3D processing software and CTan analysis software. The tibial metaphysis was chosen as a marker to select the region of the ROI, which was then analyzed and calculated using CTvol software. Specific parameters analyzed include: BV/TV; Tb.Th (mm); Tb.N (1/mm); Tb.Sp (mm), and porosity.

After Micro-CT scanning, knee samples were decalcified by placing them in 10 % EDTA for 6 weeks with fluid changes every 2 days. The completion of decalcification is measured by the ability of a syringe to easily pierce the bone tissue. After completion of decalcification, the knee joints were subjected to graded alcohol dehydration, xylene clearing, and wax impregnation followed by paraffin embedding. Knee tissue sections were 4 μm thick. Sections were routinely dewaxed and dehydrated, and subjected to HE staining, safranin O-fast green staining, and toluidine blue staining according to the instructions [45] , [46] . After staining was completed, neutral resin glue was used to seal the sections. Selected intact sections of the articular surfaces were photographed under an Olympus microscope. The knee sections were scored by two independent observers according to the criteria of Mankin score and OARSI score respectively. The mean value of the two groups was taken as the final score.

Rat primary chondrocytes were extracted from each group at different time points after ACLT (0w, 4w, 8w and 12w). The cells were rinsed three times using phosphate buffer solution (pre-cooled at 4 °C) to remove residual medium. Metabolic activity of the cells was aborted using 3 ml of methanol (−80 °C pre-cooled). Cells were scraped off with a cell scraper and collected into 15 mL centrifuge tubes for biphasic extraction with methanol: chloroform: water = 4:4:2.85 (v/v). The aqueous phase was freeze-dried. The lyophilized metabolite powder was dissolved in 550 μL of phosphate buffer (50 mM PO 4 3- , 0.05 mM TSP, pH = 7.4) and transferred to a 5 mm NMR tube for subsequent 1 H NMR-based metabolomics analysis [32] . Serum metabolomics was processed similarly to cellular metabolomics [32] . 250 µL of serum was mixed with 250 µL of 50 mM phosphate buffer in an Eppendorf tube. The samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. 500 µL of the supernatant was transferred to a 5 mm NMR tube and centrifuged at low speed (1000 r/min) for 5 min at room temperature, followed by 1 H NMR-based metabolomics analysis. NMR spectra were acquired using a Bruker Avance III 850 MHz NMR spectrometer. The experimental temperature was 298 K. The pulse sequence NOESYGPPR1D [RD-G1-90°-t-90°-τm-G2-90°-ACQ], with a relaxation delay (RD) of 2 s, a short delay (t) of 4 μs, and a mixing time (τm) of 10 ms. Using a spectral width of 20 ppm, a total of 128 transients were collected into 64 k data points with an acquisition time of 1.93 s, an additional RD of 4 s, and 64 scans. Phase correction, baseline correction and calibration were performed on all 1D NMR spectra using MestReNova software (version 9.0). The methyl peak of the TSP was used as a baseline for chemical shift correction. The water peak region at 4.70 to 4.85 ppm was excised to eliminate the distortion caused by the water peak resonance. The region of the 1D 1 H NMR spectrum with ppm of 0.50 to 9.50 was segmented with a width of 0.001 ppm and integrated. Isolated peaks or non-overlapping resonances for each metabolite were selected to calculate the metabolite integrals. The integrals of the spectral peaks were normalized to the sum of the peak integrals of the full spectrum to indicate the relative abundance of the specified metabolite. The 2D 1 H– 13 C heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) spectrum has a spectral width of 10 ppm in the 1 H direction and 110 ppm in the 13 C direction, with a data matrix of 1024 × 128 points and an RD of 1.5 s. The 2D 1 H– 1 H total correlation (TOCSY) spectra have a spectral width of 10 ppm in both 1 H dimensions, with a data matrix of 2048 × 256 and an RD of 1.5 s. Multivariate analysis of the 1D 1 H NMR spectral data of the samples was performed using SIMCA-P software (version 12.0.1). Normalized NMR spectral data were subjected to Pareto scaling, followed by unsupervised principal component analysis (PCA) and supervised orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) to examine grouping trends and reveal metabolic differences. The robustness of the OPLS-DA model was tested by a cross-validation response alignment test (200 trials). NMR spectra of metabolites were fingerprinted using Chenomx NMR Suite (version 8.6) and the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB, https://www.hmdb.ca/ ).

The results were statistically analyzed using SPSS software (version 19.0). Data are expressed as mean ± SD. p < 0.05 was used as the criterion for a statistically significant difference. In the OPLS-DA model, metabolites with VIP ≥ 1 were considered as significant metabolites. Metabolites that also satisfied p < 0.05 and VIP ≥ 1 were characterized metabolites. Metabolic pathways that received significant modulation on the postoperative time course of ACLT were analyzed using the MetaboAnalyst Web server (version 5.0) to identify metabolic pathways that were significantly altered (p < 0.05 and pathway impact value (PIV) > 0.2). PIV was calculated adding up the importance measures of each of the matched metabolites and then dividing by the sum of the importance measures of all metabolites in each pathway. The larger the value of “pathway impact”, the better, suggesting that it is more likely to be a key pathway.

Wild-type newborn C57BL/6 mice knee cartilage was extracted using sterilized surgical instruments [46] . Cartilage pellets were washed three times using pre-cooled 1 × PBS with 1 % penicillin and streptomycin added. Chondrocyte pellets were digested using trypsin for 30 min, followed by type II collagenase for 6 h. Digestion was terminated by adding four times the volume of complete medium containing 10 % fetal bovine serum in the digestion solution. The supernatant was discarded after centrifugation (350 g, 5 min). The chondrocyte precipitate was resuspended, counted and inoculated into a 10 cm dish. Primary chondrocytes were passaged to p2-p3 generation for use. Primary chondrocytes were identified by toluidine blue staining and immunofluorescence staining for COL-II protein expression (As shown in Fig. S10 ).

The primary chondrocytes of P2 generation were prepared into a single cell suspension and added to a 96 well plate with 5000 cells per well. Chondrocytes were tested for CCK8 at the end of the intervention [46] . Each group is equipped with 3 parallel secondary holes. 10 % CKK-8 solution was added to each well and incubated for 1 h. Finally, Microplate reader was used to measure the optical density (OD) values of each well at 450 nm.

Total RNA was extracted using the Trizol method according to the instructions [46] . Nucleic acid analyzer was used to detect the RNA concentration of the samples. According to the Takara Reverse Transcription Kit instructions, 2 μg of total RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA, and then 1 μL of cDNA was used as a template for mRNA amplification of each gene. Amplification conditions: pre-denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, denaturation at 95 °C for 5 s, and annealing at 60 °C for 30 s. A total of 40 cycles were performed. The mRNA expression of the target gene was calculated using the 2 -ΔΔct method.

Operations were performed according to the Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime, C1062S) instructions [47] . The primary chondrocytes were washed three times with PBS solution. Pancreatin was used to digest cells, followed by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 min. After centrifugation, the supernatant was discarded. Then, PBS solution was used to resuspend cell precipitation and then centrifuge again. After discarding the supernatant, PBS solution was used to resuspend cells into flow cytometry tubes after filtration using a cell filter. The Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime, C1062S) was used to detect apoptosis in primary chondrocytes. FIITC and PI fluorescent channels were selected to label the apoptotic state according to the reagent instructions. According to the reagent instructions, the FIITC and PI fluorescence channels of the BD FACSCanto flow cytometry were selected to label the apoptotic state.

The medium in the six-well plate was discarded and washed three times using 1 × PBS solution. Total protein was extracted by adding RIPA lysis buffer containing protease inhibitor PMSF [45] , [46] . Protein concentration was determined using a BCA kit (Servicebio, G2026-200T). Total protein was separated by SDS-PAGE electrophoresis and transferred to PVDF membrane. The PVDF membrane was blocked with BSA at room temperature for 2 h. The membrane was washed with TBST at room temperature on a shaker 3 times for 7 min each time. The corresponding primary antibodies of the target proteins were added separately and placed in a shaker at 4 °C for overnight incubation. Subsequently, the PVDF membrane was washed three times using TBST at room temperature on a shaker for 7 min each time. Incubate for 1–2 h at room temperature on a shaker using the corresponding secondary antibody depending on the species of antibody reaction. At the end of the incubation, the PVDF membrane was again washed three times with TBST for 7 min each. The final exposure was developed using a gel imaging processing system. The use of antibodies is shown in Table 2 . The grayscale values were counted using Image J software.

Antibodies.

Chondrocytes were harvested at the end of the intervention to be used for transmission electron microscopy examination according to the instructions [45] . In brief, primary chondrocytes were inoculated into six-well plates. After growth to 50 %-60 % fusion, the reagents required for the experiment were added. After intervention, the cells were washed three times with PBS and 2 ml of glutaraldehyde fixative was added to each well. After fixation for 5 min at room temperature, the cells were scraped off in one direction with a cell scraper and transferred to 1.5 ml EP tubes. Subsequently, all samples were sent to Wuhan Sevier Biotechnology Co. for subsequent transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and photography.

Operations were performed according to the kit (Elabscience, E-CK-A301) instructions [48] . Primary chondrocytes were inoculated into 12-well plates. 1 ml of cell culture medium was added to each well. After growth to 50 %-60 % fusion, the reagents required for the experiment were added. After intervention, 1 μl of CCCP (final concentration of 50 μM) was added to each well in the positive control group. The culture medium was gently shaken and incubated in cell culture medium for 5 min. The experimental group added 10 μl of JC-1 (final concentration of 2 μM) per well. The 12-well plate was placed into the cell culture medium and incubated for 15–20 min. The supernatant was aspirated at the end of incubation and washed twice with PBS. 500 μl of PBS was added to each well and observed and photographed using a fluorescence microscope.

Operations were performed according to the kit (Elabscience, E-BC-F003) instructions [49] . Briefly, the fluorescent probe was first diluted to 5 μmol/L using basal medium. Cells in each group were washed three times with PBS at the end of the intervention. Positive control reagents were added and incubated in the cell culture incubator for 30–60 min. Subsequently, 5 μmol/L of fluorescent probe was added to each well of a 12-well plate after three washes in PBS. The 12-well plates were again incubated in a cell culture incubator for 30–60 min. At the end of the incubation, PBS was again used to wash three times. Finally, the fluorescence was observed under a fluorescence microscope and photographed after adding complete medium to the 12-well plate.

Chondrocytes were inoculated into six-well plates. At the end of drug treatment, Fe 2+ concentration was measured using Ferrous ion colourimetric assay kit (Elabscience, E-BC-K881-M) [50] . PBS was used to wash the cells three times. 0.25 % trypsin was used to digest the cells down and centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min. Cells were resuspended using PBS and centrifuged again. Subsequently, 0.2 ml of Reagent 1 was added to lysate the cells by incubation on ice for 10 min, followed by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was taken for assay. Fe 2+ standards were used to configure different concentrations of Fe 2+ as standard curve as per instructions. 80 μl of standard samples/ samples to be tested were added to a 96-well plate. Subsequently, an equal volume of colour development solution was added and then incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. Finally, a spectrophotometer was used to determine the absorbance at 593 nm.

The Gpx4 gene knockdown plasmid was obtained from HanHeng Biotechnology Co (China). The siRNA of OGT gene was obtained from HeYuan Biotechnology Co Ltd (China). Both shRNA of Gpx4 gene and siRNA of OGT gene were knocked down by liposomal cell transfection. Cell transfection was performed according to the instructions of LipoFiter Liposome Transfection Reagent (Hanheng, HE-LF-1000) [45] . Briefly, chondrocytes were inoculated into six-well plates. Transfection was performed when the cells reached 50–70 % fusion. The transfection reagent was returned to room temperature. 4 μg of plasmid DNA (siRNA was 50 nM) was added to 250 μl of DMEM basal medium in a 1.5 ml centrifuge tube, while 10 μl of LipoFiter was added to 250 μl of DMEM basal medium in another 1.5 ml centrifuge tube. Two 1.5 ml centrifuge tubes were mixed and incubated at room temperature for 20 min. Subsequently, 500 μl of the mixed liquid was added to the six-well plate, followed by 1.5 ml of complete medium. The six-well plates were placed into a cell culture incubator for 6–12 h before being changed to normal medium. Cell transfection efficiency was observed using fluorescence microscopy. Finally, cell proteins were extracted after 72 h for subsequent assays.

The pHBLV-CMV-MCS-3flag-EF1-puro vector was used to construct a plasmid for OGT gene overexpression. Molecular cloning was performed according to traditional methods followed by sequencing analysis. Sequencing results consistent with the sequence of OGT gene indicated that the target plasmid was constructed successfully. Subsequently, the plasmids were extracted and purified according to the extraction kit instructions [51] . The triple plasmid lentiviral system (vector plasmid carrying the OGT gene, psPAX2 vector and pMD2G vector) was used for virus packaging. Lipofiter TM transfection reagent (HanHeng, China) was used to transfect the triple plasmid into 293 T cells. Virus supernatants were collected at 48 and 72 h after transfection. Subsequently, ultracentrifugation was used to concentrate and purify the lentivirus to obtain high titers. Dilution counting assay was used for lentiviral titer detection. Then, ATDC5 cell line was used to inoculate into six-well plates. Gradient lentiviral infection was performed when the cell density reached about 60 %. The virus-infected fluid was discarded after 24 h to replace the complete medium. Puromycin was used to screen cells successfully infected with the virus. Finally, the validation of infection efficiency was carried out by RT-qPCR and WB experiments.

Cartilage tissue from OA patients/mouse knee joint were decalcified after PFA fixation. Complete decalcification was defined by the ability of the needle tip to easily penetrate the sample. Subsequently, paraffin embedding and serial sectioning were routinely performed. Suitable slices were selected for immunohistochemical/immunofluorescence staining [45] . Antigen was repaired overnight at 60 °C using sodium citrate buffer (Beyotime, P0083). Rinse 3 times using PBS. Triton 100 was added dropwise in 10 min and rinsed 3 times using PBS. Subsequently, the closure solution (Beyotime, P0260) was used for 1 h and rinsed 3 times with PBS. Primary antibodies were added dropwise to the sections and incubated overnight at 4 °C in the refrigerator. The secondary antibody was added dropwise after PBS × 3 washes and incubated for 1–2 h at room temperature. Immunohistochemical staining was performed according to the operating instructions of the Immunohistochemistry Kit and DAB Color Development Kit. Hematoxylin stain was used to stain the nuclei of the cells. For immunofluorescence, a fluorescent-containing secondary antibody was used for incubation followed by blocking with a DAPI-containing antifluorescent bursting agent. Finally, the slices were observed under a fluorescence microscope and photographed. Analysis was performed using Image J to assess the positive expression of proteins.

Toluidine blue O staining was performed according to the kit (Solarbio, G3660) instructions [46] . Chondrocytes were inoculated into six-well plates. After removing the complete medium, the chondrocytes were washed three times using 1X PBS solution. After removing the 1X PBS solution from the six-well plates, chondrocytes were fixed using 4 % paraformaldehyde for 10–15 min. Subsequently, 4 % paraformaldehyde solution was removed and 1X PBS was used to wash the chondrocytes three times. Finally, staining was performed using a toluidine blue staining solution. After staining for 5–10 min, the coloration of chondrocytes was observed under light microscope and photographed.

Statistical processing was performed using SPSS 20.0 statistical software. Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (x ± s). Independent samples t-tests were performed for differences between the two groups, while one-way ANOVA was used for comparison of means between multiple groups. If the variance was aligned, further two-by-two comparisons were made using the LSD method. If the variance was not homogeneous, Kruska-WallisH test was used. p < 0.05 was considered a statistically significant difference.
sections.results:
As shown in Fig. 1 a, gross observations of rats at different time points showed that cartilage damage progressively worsened with increasing time after ACLT. Further, pathological sections of rat knee from each group were stained with safranin O-fast green and HE staining. As shown in Fig. 1 b-c, rats in the ACLT group showed significant cartilage loss with articular surface roughness and fissures at 8 weeks postoperatively compared to rats in the Sham group. The 12w-20w ACLT group showed a significant increase in cartilage degeneration with increasing time. The OARSI score ( Fig. 1 d) and the Mankin score ( Fig. 1 e) results further confirmed that the cartilage damage progressively worsened in the ACLT group as time progressed. In addition, toluidine blue staining result revealed that the number of subchondral bone resorption lacunae within the unit area of rats in the 20w ACLT group was significantly higher than that in the 20w Sham group ( Fig. S1 a-b). Moreover, subchondral bone morphology changes were evaluated by analyzing the medial and lateral tibial plateau of the rat knee using micro-CT ( Fig. S1 c and Supplementary table 1-2 ). In the 16w ACLT group, BV/TV and Tb.Th were significantly lower than that of the 16w Sham group, while porosity was significantly higher. The lateral subchondral bone changes of the tibial plateau were more pronounced in the 20w ACLT group, with BV/TV and Tb.Th being significantly lower than that of the 20w Sham group, whereas Tb.Sp with porosity was significantly higher than that of the 20w Sham group. Further, rat chondrocytes and serum from each group of rats at 0, 4, 8, and 12 weeks after ACLT surgery were collected for metabolomic analysis to identify key metabolic molecules involved in the initiation and progression of PTOA. Unfortunately, the number of chondrocytes extracted from rats at 16 w and 20 w after ACLT surgery was insufficient for metabolomic analysis, resulting in a lack of metabolomic data for the 16 and 20 weeks ACLT groups. We found that the cell viability of primary chondrocytes gradually decreased with the increase in the weekly age of the rats. Primary chondrocytes extracted from 0w, 4w, and 8w postoperative rats could be expanded normally to the p3 generation. However, at 16w postoperatively and 20w postoperatively after ACLT, the extracted primary chondrocytes essentially lost their proliferative ability after expansion to the p2 generation, which made the number of cells obtained insufficient for metabolomics analysis. All results of chondrocyte metabolomics analysis are shown ( Fig. 2 a-c and Fig. S2 ). For the serum metabolomics results, only the expression changes of taurine were shown ( Fig. 2 d). For rat primary chondrocyte metabolomics, 37 metabolites were identified based on the metabolite database and software for 1 H NMR spectroscopy and confirmed by 2D 1 H– 13 C HSQC and 1 H– 1 H TOCSY spectra( Fig. 2 a-d). Enrichment analysis was conducted on metabolic pathways significantly regulated in the postoperative time course of ACLT using KEGG database and web server MetaboAnalyst. A total of 9 significantly changed metabolic pathways were obtained, of which taurine and hypotaurine metabolism were one of the most significantly changed metabolic pathways. Thus, we separately analyzed the content of taurine in chondrocytes and serum. Notablely, the relative level of taurine in chondrocytes decreased 4 weeks after surgery, and then increased significantly 8 weeks after surgery ( Fig. 2 c). On the contrary, the content of taurine in serum was significantly increased at 4 W after surgery, and significantly decreased at 8w after surgery ( Fig. 2 d). We speculate that taurine in rat cartilage was depleted to a lesser extent in the early stages of OA (4 w postoperatively) and that serum taurine was transiently elevated due to feedback regulation to compensate for taurine depletion in cartilage. Furthermore, circulating blood from OA patients (65 year old men, n = 25) and healthy individuals (65 year old men, n = 30) was obtained to assay serum taurine levels. The results showed that blood taurine levels in OA patients were significantly lower than in healthy people of the same sex and age ( Fig. 2 e). Thus, we found that the small molecule metabolite taurine may be involved in the initiation and progression of OA induced by ACLT.

As taurine showed differential expression during cartilage degeneration, we hypothesise that taurine supplementation may be a potential strategy to alleviate cartilage damage. CCK8, RT-qPCR, and WB assay were used to exploring the optimal concentrations of interlukin-1β (IL-1β) and taurine in chondrocytes ( Fig. S3 ). The drug dose determined in the above experiments was used: 100 mM of taurine to protect against IL-1β-induced chondrocyte injury at 10 ng/ml. As shown in Fig. 3 a, taurine significantly reversed IL-1β-induced up-regulation of mRNA for matrix metalloproteinase-13 (MMP-13) and IL-6 in chondrocytes. Moreover, taurine significantly promoted the mRNA expression of Nrf2 and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1). Western blot analysis further validated the above results ( Fig. 3 b-c). Then, flow cytometric analysis revealed that taurine significantly inhibited IL-1β-induced chondrocyte apoptosis ( Fig. 3 d). Subsequently, transcriptomics (taurine-treated vs. non-treated in IL-1β induced chondrocytes) was used to initially clarify the potential mechanisms by which taurine protects against inflammatory chondrocyte injury in vitro ( Fig. 3 e-g). Signaling pathway enrichment analysis showed that after taurine treatment, the phenotypes of O-GlcNAcylation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammatory response appeared to be significantly altered in inflammatory chondrocytes ( Fig. 3 e). Moreover, we took the intersection of the differential genes detected by transcriptomics with the collection of genes for ferroptosis ( Fig. 3 f). The results showed the presence of four ferroptosis genes among the differential genes of transcriptomics, which initially revealed that taurine may be associated with the regulation of ferroptosis at the gene transcription level. Further, bioinformatics analysis was used for signaling pathway enrichment analysis of taurine-predicted target proteins revealed that processes such as ferroptosis and TP53 signaling may be regulated by taurine ( Fig. 3 g). In addition, metabolomics (taurine-treated vs. non-treated in IL-1β induced chondrocytes) was also used to clarify the potential mechanisms by which taurine protects against inflammatory chondrocyte injury in vitro ( Fig. 3 h-i). As taurine is widely known as a potent antioxidant, we focused on the role of taurine on the regulation of O-GlcNAcylation and ferroptosis in inflammatory chondrocytes, which has not been previously reported. Therefore, we hypothesized that the alleviation of chondrocyte inflammation by taurine may be related to the regulation of O-GlcNAcylation and ferroptosis.

Taurine alleviates IL-β-induced chondrocyte injury. ( a: Protective effect of taurine on IL-1β-induced chondrocyte injury by RT-qPCR; b-c: Protective effect of taurine against IL-1β-induced chondrocyte injury by WB; d: The effect of taurine on IL-1β-induced chondrocyte apoptosis was analyzed by flow cytometry; e: Signaling pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes between taurine-treated and non-treated groups by transcriptomics; f: the intersection of the differential genes detected by transcriptomics with the collection of genes for ferroptosis; g: Signaling pathway enrichment analysis of target proteins of taurine by bioinformatics analysis; h-i: Signaling pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed metabolites between taurine-treated and non-treated groups by metabolomics. n = 3, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01).

Based on the above findings, we tentatively determined that Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis may be a key mechanism by which taurine alleviates inflammatory injury in chondrocytes. As shown in Fig. 4 a, IL-1β significantly inhibited the expression of Gpx4 and solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) proteins and promoted the expression of prostaglandin endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2), solute carrier family 40 member 1(SLC40A1), and p53 proteins in chondrocytes, suggesting that IL-1β induced chondrocyte ferroptosis, whereas taurine supplementation partially reversed the expression of IL-1β-induced ferroptosis-related proteins in chondrocytes. The transmission electron microscopy results also confirmed that taurine supplementation could protect chondrocyte ferroptosis ( Fig. 4 b). In addition, the results of mitochondrial membrane potential detection by JC-1 showed that taurine could inhibit the IL-1β-induced increase in mitochondrial membrane potential ( Fig. 4 c-d). The results of lipid peroxidation ( Fig. 4 e-f) and Fe 2+ concentration ( Fig. 4 g) assay also support the antioxidant effect of taurine. Further, FIN56 ( Fig. 4 h), a small molecule inhibitor of Gpx4, and shRNA for Gpx4 ( Fig. 4 i-j) were used to inhibit protein expression of Gpx4 in chondrocytes to verify whether inhibition of Gpx4 partially reversed the protective effect of taurine on inflammatory chondrocytes, respectively. The results showed that inhibition of Gpx4 significantly suppressed the protein expression of ACAN and promoted the protein expression of MMP13, suggesting that taurine may alleviate inflammatory alterations of chondrocytes by modulating Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis. In addition, taurine has been widely studied for its potent antioxidant properties. Our results also demonstrated that taurine could inhibit chondrocyte inflammatory injury through Nrf2/HO-1 signaling ( Fig. S4 ). Importantly, this regulatory mechanism may be related to ferroptosis ( Fig. S4 ), as cumulative evidence that Nrf2/HO-1/Gpx4 is a classical ferroptosis signaling pathway. The above results demonstrated that taurine can alleviate chondrocyte ferroptosis by promoting Gpx4 expression.

GlcNAcylation is regulated by two conserved enzymes: O-GlcNAc enzyme (OGA), which can remove O-GlcNAc from proteins, and O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT), which can add O-GlcNAc to proteins. To validate the involvement of O-GlcNAcylation in regulating pathological changes in OA, mildly/severely damaged cartilage from OA patients were obtained to examine the expression of OGT and total O-GlcNAcylation levels. We found higher expression of OGT and total O-GlcNAcylation levels in mildly damaged cartilage from OA patients compared to severely damaged cartilage ( Fig. 5 a). This suggests reduced levels of O-GlcNAcylation in OA cartilage tissue. Moreover, IL-1β treatment suppressed OGT and O-GlcNAc in chondrocytes in a concentration-dependent manner ( Fig. 5 b). Therefore, we speculate that modulation of O-GlcNAcylation levels may influence chondrocyte metabolism.

Taurine protects against IL-1β-induced primary chondrocyte injury by increasing O-GlcNAcylation. ( a: Saffron O-fast green staining and expression of COL-II, O-GlcNAc (Red labeled) and OGT (Green labeled) proteins in mildly/severely damaged cartilage from OA patients; b: Altered protein expression of O-GlcNAc and OGT in chondrocytes after treatment with different concentrations of IL-1β by WB; c: Alterations in chondrocyte metabolic marker expression after OSMI/TMG treatment in chondrocytes with or without IL-1β induction by WB; d: Alterations in chondrocyte metabolic marker expression and ferroptosis markers after OSMI/TMG treatment in IL-1β-induced chondrocytes with or without taurine treatment by WB; e: Alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential after OSMI/TMG treatment in IL-1β-induced chondrocytes with or without taurine treatment by JC-1; f: Alterations in lipid peroxides after OSMI/TMG treatment in IL-1β-induced chondrocytes with or without taurine treatment by lipid peroxide detection kit; g: Alterations in the concentration of Fe 2+ after OSMI/TMG treatment in IL-1β-induced chondrocytes with or without taurine treatment by Fe 2+ colorimetric assay kit. n = 3, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01).

TMG, promoting O-GlcNAc modification, and OSMI-1, inhibiting O-GlcNAc modification, were used to treat chondrocytes. We found that OSMI treatment was able to significantly inhibit the protein expression of ACAN, while TMG treatment was able to significantly promote the expression of MMP13 in chondrocytes ( Fig. 5 c). Further, OSMI treatment partially reversed the upregulation of ACAN by taurine, whereas TMG further enhanced the promotion of ACAN by taurine in IL-1β-induced chondrocytes ( Fig. 5 d). Importantly, OSMI partially reversed the inhibitory effect of taurine on ferroptosis-associated proteins such as p53, PTGS2, and SLC40A1, while TMG further enhanced the inhibitory effect of taurine on ferroptosis, suggesting that OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation may be involved in mediating the regulation of chondrocyte ferroptosis by taurine. To provide more evidence, mitochondrial membrane potential and lipid peroxidation levels of chondrocytes were examined after treatment with OSMI/TMG. OSMI treatment inhibited the ameliorative effects of taurine on mitochondrial membrane potential ( Fig. 5 e) and lipid peroxidation ( Fig. 5 f) in chondrocytes, whereas TMG treatment promoted the ameliorative effects of taurine on mitochondrial membrane potential and lipid peroxidation in chondrocytes. Ferrous ion concentration assay results also showed that O-GlcNAcylation may be involved in the regulation of ferroptosis due to OSMI up-regulated Fe 2+ concentration while TMG down-regulated Fe 2+ concentration in chondrocytes ( Fig. 5 g). Moreover, since OSMI treatment did not alter the protein expression level of OGT, siRNA was used to knock down OGT expression in primary chondrocytes. Additionally, lentiviral infections were used to construct cells stably overexpressing the OGT gene ( Fig. S5 ). We found that knocking down OGT expression partially reversed the protective effect of taurine on chondrocytes by inhibiting protein expression of ACAN and promoting MMP13 expression ( Fig. 6 a), whereas overexpression of OGT played the opposite role( Fig. 6 b). The above results demonstrated the ability of taurine to alleviate Gpx4-dependent chondrocyte ferroptosis by promoting O-GlcNAcylation.

OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation mediates the protective effect of taurine on inflammatory chondrocytes. ( a: Effect of knockdown of OGT protein expression on chondrocyte metabolic markers by WB; b: Effect of overexpression of OGT protein expression on chondrocyte metabolic markers by WB. n = 3, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01).

Since O-GlcNAcylation is a ubiquitous post-translational modification of proteins, we speculated that Gpx4, the key protein in ferroptosis, may have O-GlcNAc modification sites. Thus, we predicted the O-GlcNAc modification sites of Gpx4 protein by YinOYang wedsite ( https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/YinOYang-1.2/ ). As shown in Fig. S6 a-b, the ferroptosis marker Gpx4 protein may contain multiple O-GlcNAc modification sites. Therefore, we speculated that taurine may protect against chondrocyte inflammatory injury by alleviating chondrocyte ferroptosis through modulation of Gpx4 O-GlcNAcylation. Since O-GlcNAcylation is regulated by OGT, we speculate that Gpx4 protein may interact with OGT protein. Molecular docking demonstrated the existence of possible protein binding sites for Gpx4 and OGT ( Fig. S6 c). Moreover, TMG significantly promoted total O-GlcNAcylation levels in chondrocytes in a concentration-dependent manner ( Fig. S6 d), while OSMI significantly inhibited total O-GlcNAcylation levels in chondrocytes in a concentration-dependent manner ( Fig. S6 e). Importantly, Gpx4 protein expression gradually elevated with increasing TMG concentration in chondrocytes ( Fig. S6 d), whereas Gpx4 protein expression gradually declined with increasing OSMI concentration in chondrocytes ( Fig. S6 e).

To verify that OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation promotes Gpx4 stability, CHX was used to block protein synthesis in chondrocytes. We found that Gpx4 expression gradually decreased with increasing CHX treatment time ( Fig. 7 a). OSMI accelerated the degradation of Gpx4 ( Fig. 7 a), whereas TMG slowed down the degradation of Gpx4 ( Fig. 7 b). Moreover, knockdown of OGT expression accelerated Gpx4 degradation ( Fig. 7 c), whereas overexpression of OGT inhibited Gpx4 degradation ( Fig. 7 d). Also, the addition of MG132 provided further evidence that O-GlcNAcylation can promote the stability of Gpx4 protein ( Fig. 7 e-g). The underlying mechanism may be related to ubiquitination inhibition ( Fig. 7 h). Subsequently, we preliminarily verified the possible presence of O-GlcNAcylation of the Gpx4 protein by immunoprecipitation ( Fig. 7 i). Finally, immunoprecipitation ( Fig. 7 j-k) and immunofluorescence ( Fig. 7 l) results verified the possible interaction between OGT and Gpx4 proteins. The above findings indicated that OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation may stabilize Gpx4 expression by inhibiting ubiquitination degradation.

OGT promotes Gpx4 protein stability. (a-b: Effect of OSMI/TMG on Gpx4 protein degradation by WB after CHX (1 μM) treatment at different time points; c-d: Effect of knockdown/overexpression of OGT on Gpx4 protein degradation by WB after CHX (1 μM) treatment at different time points; e: Effect of OSMI/TMG on Gpx4 protein degradation in the presence or absence of MG132; f-g: Effect of knockdown/overexpression of OGT on Gpx4 protein degradation in the presence or absence of MG132; h: Immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate possible O-GlcNAcylation of Gpx4 protein; i-k: Immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate possible interaction between Gpx4 protein and OGT protein; l: Immunofluorescence experiments demonstrate possible interaction between Gpx4 protein and OGT protein. n = 3, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01).

Finally, animal experiments were performed to verify that OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation and Gpx4-dependent Ferroptosis mediate the protective effects of taurine against cartilage degeneration. ACLT was used to construct a mouse PTOA animal model ( Fig. S7 a). Gpx4 protein expression was inhibited in cartilage by articular cavity injection of AAV-shRNA-Gpx4. O-GlcNAcylation levels in cartilage tissue were inhibited/promoted by joint cavity injection of OSMI and TMG, respectively. All three agents, taurine, OSMI and TMG, were administered through the joint cavity every three days. All mice were sacrificed eight weeks after ACLT. There was no significant difference in the body weight of mice in each group before sacrifice ( Fig. S7 b). Although the knee joints of mice in the ACLT group, ACLT + Taur + AAV-sh-Gpx4 group, and ACLT + Taur + OSMI group appeared to be significantly swollen, knee joint dimension measurements showed no significant differences among the groups of mice ( Fig. S7 c). However, dissecting the knee joint capsule revealed rough articular cartilage surfaces and obvious cartilage defects in the mice in the ACLT group ( Fig. S7 d). Compared to the ACLT group, the cartilage surface of mice in the ACLT + Taur group was smooth and showed only mild obscuration. Mice in the ACLT + Taur + AAV-sh-Gpx4 and ACLT + Taur + OSMI groups also showed significant damage to the cartilage surface, especially the articular cartilage of mice in the ACLT + Taur + AAV-sh-Gpx4 group showed swelling and significant loss of cartilage layer. Further, mouse gait analysis by Catwalk showed that the average speed, maximum contact intensity and swing speed of mice in the ACLT group were significantly reduced, suggesting that the mice may have experienced pain during walking due to knee injury ( Fig. S8 ). However, taurine administration partially reversed the reduction in the above metrics. Inhibition of Gpx4 and O-GlcNAcylation, on the other hand, impaired the pain-relieving effects of taurine in PTOA mice. In addition, osteophyte formation is an indirect response to pain in PTOA mice. Micro-CT was used to visualize bone morphologic changes in mouse knee joints. As shown in Fig. S9 a, osteophyte formation was less in the ACLT + Taur group than in the ACLT group, while inhibition of Gpx4 and O-GlcNAcylation exacerbated osteophyte formation in the mouse knee. Moreover, the subchondral bones of mouse tibia and femur were separated for 3D reconstruction to analyze bone morphometric changes ( Fig. S9 a-c). Consistent with our previous findings, ACLT accelerated bone loss in subchondral bone. Taurine administration can exert a protective effect on subchondral bone remodeling in PTOA mice. The findings were further supported by the results of HE staining ( Fig. 8 a-b) and saffron O/fast green staining ( Fig. 8 c-d) of mouse knee joints. Type II collagen is a major component of the cartilage matrix. We found that taurine was able to reduce the loss of type II collagen in the cartilage matrix in ACLT-induced PTOA mice, whereas inhibition of Gpx4 and O-GlcNAcylation impaired this protective effect of taurine ( Fig. 8 e-f). Importantly, we found for the first time that both OGT and total O-GlcNAc protein expression were significantly decreased in articular cartilage of PTOA mice, whereas taurine was able to upregulate both OGT and total O-GlcNAc protein expression in PTOA mice ( Fig. 9 a). Inhibition of O-GlcNAcylation via OSMI and promotion of O-GlcNAcylation via TMG impaired and enhanced the protective effects of taurine against cartilage degeneration in ACLT-induced PTOA mice, respectively. It is suggested that OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation may be a potential mechanism by which taurine protects against cartilage degeneration. In addition, previous studies reported that Gpx4-dependent chondrocyte ferroptosis contributed to OA cartilage degeneration. Our study found that taurine was able to upregulate Gpx4 expression in articular cartilage of PTOA mice, whereas inhibition of Gpx4 expression impaired the protective effect of taurine on chondrocytes ( Fig. 9 b), suggesting that Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis may be another potential mechanism by which taurine protects against cartilage degeneration in addition to OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation.

sections.discussion:
OA is the most common musculoskeletal disease among people over the age of 60, affecting over 650 million people worldwide [28] . The diffuse inflammatory state inside the joint can break the dynamic equilibrium of articular cartilage anabolism and catabolism, which is manifested as cartilage degeneration [29] . Currently, the relationship between abnormal cartilage metabolism and the progression of OA is not fully understood. The analysis of key metabolic molecules and related metabolic pathways from a metabolic perspective are receiving increasing attention [30] , [31] . Metabolomics can not only reveal the pathogenesis of OA from a metabolic perspective, but also help screen biomarkers for early diagnosis of OA, providing evidence for early diagnosis of the disease. Thus, to screen out key metabolic molecules in the pathogenesis of OA, we constructed PTOA models of rats at different weeks of age (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 weeks) after ACLT surgery and conducted relevant metabolomics analysis. The results of both changes in articular cartilage and subchondral bone demonstrated the success of ACLT surgery in constructing a rat model of PTOA, and the severity of OA gradually increases over time.

Subsequently, rat knee chondrocytes and serum samples [32] were extracted for metabolomic analysis. Based on the MetaboAnalyst analysis, we finally selected taurine as the concerned metabolic molecule. Chondrocyte metabolomics demonstrated that taurine decreased (4 weeks, p < 0.01) and then increased (8 weeks, p < 0.01) in chondrocytes of rats after ACLT, whereas serum metabolomics revealed that taurine increased (4 weeks, p < 0.01) and then decreased (8 and 12 weeks, p < 0.01) in the serum of rats after ACLT. We propose a hypothesis that perhaps the abnormal mechanical stress and inflammatory environment within the cartilage after ACLT resulted in a large consumption of taurine by chondrocytes to promote cartilage repair, while the body supplies and replenishes taurine to cartilage through blood circulation. In the early postoperative period after ACLT, there is a decrease in taurine content due to depletion of taurine in cartilage. With the gradual replenishment of taurine from the blood into the cartilage tissue, the cartilage tissue showed an increase in taurine concentration, whereas circulating taurine first showed a stressful upregulation at 4w and then remained stable. In addition, a recent study published in the journal Science found that taurine concentrations in the blood gradually decrease with age [27] , which partially rationalizes the decline in taurine levels in the blood after 4w. Futhermore, Yao et al. [33] found that taurine can promote chondrogenic differentiation of human cord blood mesenchymal cells. Taurine can also inhibit the dedifferentiation of chondrocytes, thus maintaining the cartilage phenotype [34] . Moreover, Cheleschi et al. [35] preliminarily revealed taurine can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD-2) and catalase (CAT) to play an antioxidant protective role and thus offset H 2 O 2 induced oxidative stress damage of chondrocytes in vitro [36] . Thus, there is limited evidence that taurine protects against cartilage damage through antioxidant effects.

In our study, transcriptomic analyses were used to further investigate the potential mechanisms by which taurine protects against cartilage degeneration. Combined with the results of signaling pathway enrichment analyses of taurine target proteins, we focused on the possibility that ferroptosis and O-GlcNAcylation may be regulated by taurine, which may be a novel mechanism by which taurine protects against cartilage damage. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent programmed cell death process characterized by the accumulation of ROS [37] . Consistent with previous findings [35] , [36] , we found that TBHQ significantly promoted the protective effect of taurine on primary chondrocytes, while ML385 partially reversed the protective effect of taurine on primary chondrocytes, suggesting that taurine can alleviate chondrocyte inflammatory injury by activating the Nrf2/HO-1 axis. In addition, oxidative stress-associated ferroptosis may also be a potential mechanism by which taurine protects against chondrocyte injury [38] . Recently, Yao et al. [39] found a direct relationship between chondrocyte ferroptosis and pathological changes in OA. Under iron overload, hyperlipidemia, or inflammatory stimuli, Gpx4 expression in chondrocytes is decreased to induce the accumulation of ROS and peroxides, which ultimately leads to chondrocyte ferroptosis, thereby accelerating OA progression [20] . Gpx4 has been reported to be a major regulator of ferroptosis [16] . In our study, we found that taurine was able to partially reverse IL-1β-induced downregulation of Gpx4, which may be related to the alleviation of ferroptosis. Knockdown of Gpx4 or FIN56 were both able to partially reverse the benefits of taurine on chondrocyte metabolism. Thus, Gpx4-mediated ferroptosis may be one of the key mechanisms by which taurine alleviates inflammatory chondrocyte injury.

O-GlcNAcylation, as an inducible, reversible and dynamic post-translational modification of proteins, can be involved in the regulation of intracellular gene expression, metabolism and immunity, cellular signaling and protein homeostasis through the modification of various functional proteins [40] . Currently, only one paper has reported the detection of elevated levels of OGT and O-GlcNAcylation in chondrocytes derived from cartilage of OA patients, suggesting that O-GlcNAcylation may be associated with the development of OA [41] . However, in our study, we found significantly lower expression of OGT and O-GlcNAc in severely injured OA cartilage tissue from OA patients compared to mildly injured OA cartilage tissue. Similarly, reduced expression of OGT and O-GlcNAc was detected in cartilage tissues of the ACLT group as well as in IL-1β-induced primary chondrocytes. The reason for this discrepancy may be the partial phenotypic alteration of the extracted human chondrocytes during passaging in that published literature. Further, we found that OSMI partially reversed the protective effect of taurine on chondrocytes, while TMG enhanced the protective effect of taurine on chondrocytes. Moreover, knockdown of OGT also attenuated the benefits of taurine on chondrocyte metabolism. This suggests that taurine may protect against chondrocyte inflammatory injury by promoting OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation. Notably, since O-GlcNAcylation is a widespread post-translational modification, we speculated that Gpx4, a key protein in ferroptosis, may have OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation. Previous studies have shown an important reciprocal regulatory role between O-GlcNAcylation and oxidative stress [42] , [43] , suggesting that O-GlcNAcylation may have a reciprocal regulatory relationship with oxidative stress-related ferroptosis. Our study also confirmed that OSMI promotes ferroptosis, whereas TMG can inhibit ferroptosis in chondrocytes, although the evidence is limited. Moreover, molecular docking, immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, and prediction of the O-GlcNAcylation site of Gpx4 showed that Gpx4 protein can interact with OGT protein. This is the first report of a reciprocal regulatory relationship between Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis and OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation, which will also provide new ideas for regulatory roles of ferroptosis in other diseases.
sections.limitations: In this experiment, we identified Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis and OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation as potential mechanisms by which taurine protects against cartilage damage in ACLT-induced PTOA. However, techniques such as immunofluorescence, immunoprecipitation, and molecular docking could not adequately demonstrate a possible direct interaction between Gpx4 and OGT. Future research could employ advanced techniques such as co-immunoprecipitation with high-resolution mass spectrometry analysis to clarify whether there are direct physical interactions or if the regulation occurs through intermediate molecules and signaling cascades. Moreover, more evidence including surface plasmon resonance and cellular thermal shift assay is also needed to fully demonstrate the existence of a direct interaction between Gpx4 and OGT proteins. Besides, future studies can combine mass spectrometry and site directed mutagenesis techniques to explore and validate the O-GlcNAcylation site of Gpx4. Gpx4 knockout mice can also be constructed in combination with site directed mutagenesis to fully validate the function of Gpx4 in cartilage degeneration. In addition, while this study focuses on the downstream effects of taurine on Gpx4 and ferroptosis, the upstream regulators that modulate the ferroptosis pathway in the context of OA are not comprehensively explored. Future endeavors can screen for potential upstream kinases, transcription factors, or microRNAs that can directly or indirectly influence Gpx4 expression and ferroptosis activation. It is worth mentioning that although we found that O-GlcNAcylation levels were reduced in OA chondrocytes, O-GlcNAcylation levels appeared to be elevated in OA hyperplastic synovial tissues (data not shown). The regulatory role of O-GlcNAcylation in OA synovial inflammatory tissues needs to be further explored, which is the next attractive research direction.
sections.conclusion:
In this study, we identified taurine, a key metabolic molecule in PTOA lesions, by metabolomic analysis of knee chondrocytes and serum from rats with ACLT-induced PTOA. IL-β-induced inflammatory and oxidative stress phenotypes in primary chondrocytes were alleviated by exogenous addition of taurine. In addition, transcriptomics and metabolomics analyses further revealed that taurine may protect against IL-1β-induced chondrocyte injury by inhibiting Gpx4-dependent ferroptosis and activating OGT-dependent O-GlcNAcylation ( Fig. 10 ). Considering that taurine is a very safe amino acid commonly used for food or pharmaceutical additions, the results of this study are expected to provide a scientific basis for possible translational research and application of taurine in PTOA therapy.
